slides.title: Order is not promised
slides.main: Without ORDER BY, the order of rows in the result is not guaranteed.

captions: While we read the whole table, rows arrive 'as written', so the order seems fixed
After an index or a condition, the order may change and the application breaks
If the order matters, ask for it explicitly: ORDER BY

frames.text:
a different order is
not a database bug

slides.title: ASC and DESC
slides.main: ASC is ascending (the default), DESC is descending.

captions: ASC is ascending, the default order
DESC is descending: the biggest values first
The sort column need not be in the select list

frames.text:
prices not shown,
but sorted by them

slides.title: Sorting text
slides.main: Strings sort byte by byte: uppercase comes before lowercase.

captions: SQLite compares strings by character codes, not 'like a human'
Uppercase Latin comes before lowercase, Cyrillic after Latin
For dictionary order, convert values to one case

frames.text:
apple and Apple
side by side

slides.title: Several keys
slides.main: The second key resolves ties on the first.

captions: With one key, products in the same category come in arbitrary order
Add a second key after a comma: within a category, by price descending
Put the id last: the order becomes unambiguous

lines: ORDER BY category, price DESC, id;

slides.title: What you can sort by
slides.main: You can sort by an expression, an alias, or a column number.

captions: A key can be an expression: the length of a name
ORDER BY runs after SELECT, so it sees the alias
You can give a column number, but it 'drifts' when the query changes

lines: SELECT price * 2 AS dbl FROM products

frames.text:
2 is the second
column of the list

slides.title: Missing values in sorting
slides.main: In SQLite NULL counts as the smallest: it comes first.

captions: In SQLite NULL is less than any value, so with ASC it comes first
With DESC, empty values end up last
NULLS FIRST and NULLS LAST set the position explicitly, without relying on defaults

lines: ORDER BY brand ASC NULLS LAST;

slides.title: LIMIT
slides.main: LIMIT n keeps the first n rows of the result.

captions: LIMIT 3 keeps the first three rows; which ones depends on the sort
If there are fewer rows, you get what exists, with no error
LIMIT 0 returns an empty result

slides.title: Top N
slides.main: ORDER BY first, LIMIT after: sort, then cut.

captions: First, ORDER BY arranges all rows by price descending
Then LIMIT 3 keeps the first three: the top expensive products
Without ORDER BY, the same three rows would be random

slides.title: OFFSET
slides.main: OFFSET skips the start: LIMIT 10 OFFSET 20 is page three.

captions: LIMIT 3 OFFSET 0: the first three rows
LIMIT 3 OFFSET 3: three rows after skipping three
LIMIT 3 OFFSET 6: offset = (page - 1) × size

lines: SELECT id FROM t ORDER BY id
SELECT id FROM t ORDER BY id
SELECT id FROM t ORDER BY id

slides.title: Pagination traps
slides.main: A big OFFSET is costly; on large tables, paginate by key.

captions: OFFSET 20000 makes the database find and throw away 20000 rows: later pages are slower
If a row is added between queries, pages shift: a row shows up twice
Keyset pagination: 'id > last seen' is equally fast every time

slides.title: DISTINCT and sorting
slides.main: Order: WHERE, DISTINCT, ORDER BY, then LIMIT.

captions: FROM → WHERE → SELECT (DISTINCT) → ORDER BY → LIMIT
DISTINCT removes repeats, ORDER BY orders the already unique values
The condition picks the category, sorting puts expensive first, limit takes three

slides.title: Second by price
slides.main: Second by price: ORDER BY price DESC LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1.

captions: Second most expensive: sort descending, skip one row, take one
If the top two prices are equal, the query returns second in order, not by value
Second distinct value: DISTINCT first, then sort and skip

slides.title: Summary
slides.main: ORDER BY sets the order, LIMIT and OFFSET cut a window from the result.

captions: ORDER BY: keys, direction, expressions, aliases, and where empty values go
LIMIT and OFFSET cut a window from the ordered result
